questions.question: Describe rapid transport systems in South Africa and evaluate them.
questions.expected_answer: Rapid transport moves many people quickly on separate routes. Bus rapid transit uses large buses in dedicated lanes with pay-before-boarding, level-boarding stations and feeder buses: Rea Vaya in Johannesburg from 2009, MyCiTi in Cape Town, A Re Yeng in Tshwane and Go George. It is cheaper and quicker to build than underground rail, avoids traffic, is frequent and accessible, but takes road space from cars, needs subsidies, does not reach every area and has caused conflict with taxi operators. The Gautrain, opened from 2010, links Johannesburg, Sandton, Pretoria and O. R. Tambo airport quickly and safely but has higher fares and limited coverage.

questions.question: Explain how subsidies and integrated tickets help public transport.
questions.expected_answer: A subsidy is government money that lowers fares or keeps a service running. Subsidies help low-income workers far from jobs afford travel, encourage people to leave cars at home, support the economy and help correct the apartheid spatial pattern; South Africa subsidises commuter buses, Metrorail and BRT, and many cities offer reduced fares for pensioners, learners and people with disabilities. Challenges include high public cost, possible waste and the fact that minibus taxis, which carry most commuters, have received little direct subsidy. Integrated tickets let commuters change between modes with one card more cheaply.

questions.question: Describe bus and cycle lanes, park and ride and car-free zones.
questions.expected_answer: Dedicated bus lanes give buses priority past traffic; cycle lanes make cycling safer if connected, lit and protected; park and ride lets drivers leave cars at the city edge or stations, such as Gautrain stations, and continue by public transport; car-free zones ban cars from streets to reduce noise and pollution, improve safety and help local shops, with planned deliveries and emergency access. Other measures include coordinated traffic lights, congestion charges, flexible working hours and mixed land use. A bus lane carrying 4 800 people an hour moves about 2.2 times as many as a car lane carrying 2 160.
